Evade Weekly / Issue 001

Can earnings carry the weight?

The Fed has paused. Inflation still matters. Our first question is whether profit growth can compensate for pressure on costs and valuations.

Draft · Founder review pending7-minute read28 October 2026

Information cutoff: 28 October 2026 · 19:50 UTC / 20:50 Zagreb / 15:50 New York.

This is a midweek working draft for discussion. The US session is still open at this cutoff. It is not a completed weekly review or a founder-approved investment view.

The opening view

A company can grow its profits while its share price falls. That is the idea behind this first issue. Investors care about the earnings a business can produce and the price they are willing to pay for those earnings. Stronger profits can be offset by a lower valuation; sufficiently strong profits can also overcome that pressure.

Our working hypothesis: earnings resilience deserves scrutiny before treating a central-bank pause as an equity buy signal. We will test revenue, margins and expectations separately. This is an analytical framework, not an established forecast for either region.

What changed: the Fed held, without an all-clear

Verified event: at 18:00 UTC on 28 October, the Federal Reserve left its target rate range at 3.75–4.00%. The vote was 10–2; the dissenters preferred a quarter-percentage-point increase. The statement described strong activity and elevated inflation. Federal Reserve, 28 October

Why it matters: an unchanged overnight policy rate does not freeze bond yields or equity valuations. Those also reflect expectations about future rates, growth and risk. The relevant question is what changed relative to what investors expected—not simply whether today’s decision was a hold.

Countercase: resilient activity can support company revenues. A rate pause need not be negative for equities if earnings expectations improve enough. We have not measured a post-announcement causal effect on stock prices here.

The equity backdrop: an early snapshot, not a closing verdict

Bloomberg’s 28 October market wrap, syndicated by SWI swissinfo, reported the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 broadly unchanged and the STOXX Europe 600 up 0.1% in its early-session snapshot. The S&P observation was timed at 09:56 New York / 13:56 UTC, before the Fed decision. The report highlighted forthcoming Microsoft and Alphabet earnings. Bloomberg via SWI: pre-decision market wrap

These are reported intraday moves, not independently reconstructed index returns. They do not describe the close, the full week or the reaction to the later Fed announcement. Their useful message for this issue is the competing focus on policy and company results.

Inflation reaches equities through more than one route

US background, released 14 October: September consumer prices rose 0.6% month on month, seasonally adjusted, and 3.7% over twelve months, unadjusted. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually. These are September observations, not fresh data released today. BLS September CPI release

Euro-area background, available 16 October: annual inflation measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) was 3.8% in September, compared with 3.2% in August. Energy prices rose 18.9% annually. HICP and US CPI use different methodologies; their headline rates are context, not a perfectly like-for-like comparison. Eurostat September inflation data

The mechanism: input costs can rise faster than a company’s selling prices, reducing its profit margin. Alternatively, a business with pricing power can pass on costs while retaining customers. Energy producers may benefit from the same price increase that hurts energy-intensive manufacturers. Company exposure matters more than a blanket claim that inflation hurts every stock.

Europe: a policy decision ahead, a company result in hand

The ECB calendar schedules its policy announcement for 29 October at 14:15 CET / 13:15 UTC. That is after this issue’s cutoff. We cannot report its decision yet. ECB weekly calendar

For a company-level test, UBS reported third-quarter net profit attributable to shareholders of USD 2.690 billion. That compares with USD 2.481 billion a year earlier, an 8.4% increase. Revenue rose while operating expenses fell, but a higher tax expense absorbed part of the pre-tax improvement. The company’s reported and underlying earnings measures must be kept separate. UBS official Q3 release, pages 12–13

The questions are how repeatable the earnings are, which revenues and costs changed, and what capital or credit losses might absorb in future. One bank’s result does not establish that all European earnings are resilient. Nor does a large profit establish a positive earnings surprise: that needs a dated consensus estimate.

A US counterexample: sales growth did not become EPS growth

Robinhood’s 27 October results reported third-quarter revenue of USD 1.424 billion, up 12%, while US accounting-standard (GAAP) diluted earnings per share (EPS) fell 16% to USD 0.51. Operating expenses rose 16%. Robinhood official results, pages 1 and 4–5

This is a useful challenge to our earnings-resilience question. Growing revenue alone did not establish improving per-share profit. Investment marks, expenses and accounting adjustments need to be reconciled; we should not attribute the entire EPS decline to inflation or costs without that bridge. Adjusted EPS is a different measure from GAAP EPS. This one company does not settle the outlook for US indices, and no share-price reaction or consensus surprise is asserted.

The theory in numbers: earnings growth versus the multiple

Illustration, not a market valuation: assume earnings per share (EPS) of $10 and a price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of 20. Price = EPS × P/E, so the share price is $200. If EPS grows 10% to $11 but the multiple falls to 18, the implied price becomes $198: a 1% decline despite higher earnings.

If EPS instead grows 15% to $11.50 at the same 18-times multiple, the price becomes $207: a 3.5% increase. To offset a move from 20 to 18 times earnings exactly, EPS must rise by 11.11%: 20/18 − 1.

A higher required return can put pressure on the multiple, but interest rates do not mechanically determine P/E. Growth expectations and perceived risk also matter. This example holds those changes inside the assumed multiple; it is not a model of fair value or a prediction of returns. Dividends are excluded.

What we will test next

Microsoft’s investor-relations calendar identifies 28 October results after the stock-market close. Our cutoff precedes that release. Microsoft investor-relations FAQ

For the earnings review, collect revenue growth, operating margin, EPS, cash generation and management’s forward guidance. Compare reported and adjusted results on the same basis. Then ask whether investment spending creates future earnings or simply consumes cash today. Only call a result a beat or miss when a time-stamped expectation is available.

The stronger case for equities would combine durable profit growth, credible cash generation and expectations that still leave room for improvement. The opposing case is that costs or capital spending absorb revenue growth while investors reduce the multiple they will pay. Neither case is settled by one release.

The BEA calendar also schedules the advance estimate of third-quarter US GDP and September personal income and outlays for 29 October at 08:30 Eastern / 12:30 UTC. These are upcoming tests, not known outcomes in this issue. BEA release schedule

The discussion behind the draft.

The question you chose: can earnings growth offset both cost pressure and valuation pressure? This draft investigates that question. It does not attribute a bullish or bearish recommendation to you. The reading key

Keep the layers separate.

Fact: a dated release or reported observation with a source.

Interpretation: a possible economic mechanism or working hypothesis.

Countercase: evidence or a scenario that could weaken the view.

Illustration: assumed numbers used to explain a concept.
